fixes.explanation: Armies sounds right with four hundred men coming, friend, and I'd have said it too. But the text says Jacob divides his people, flocks, herds and camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) Then he thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) That's a man planning for somebody to get away, so the word is camps.

That's the instruction, baker! Jacob entrusts the animals to his servants in separate herds and says, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) Picture it. Herd after herd, each one a little way behind the last, like a row of cookie sheets coming out one at a time instead of one big crowded tray. Jacob is sending gift after gift ahead of him.

problems.problem: “Not win a battle” rules out an intention the text does not address. Jacob says that if one camp is attacked, the other can escape.
“Esau meets a gift, then another gift, then another” presents the meeting as having happened. The passage only describes Jacob sending the herds ahead.
